newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: FEATURE - Malthusian warnings spawn super-rice quest.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Malthusian warnings spawn super-rice quest.

text.p: In the early 19th century, English clergyman Thomas Robert Malthus predicted that the world's population would eventually outstrip its resources.
Many economists continue to subscribe to Malthus' grim prophecy today, but researchers in the sleepy Philippine town of Los Banos are out to prove them wrong.

For more than 25 years, the International Rice Research Centre (IRRI) has been working on identifying more high-yielding varieties of rice -- the staple of more than half of humanity. In that time, its research has been credited with increasing average rice yields by 71 percent. More than 60 percent of the world's rice paddies are planted with varieties developed at the IRRI and their progenies.
Much of Asia, where 92 percent of the world's rice is grown, is now self-sufficient and many countries have exportable surpluses.
But with the prospect of at least four billion rice eaters by the year 2025, the IRRI is working on a new "super-rice", which can increase average yields by a further 25 percent.
"The plant is now being designed. The architecture is there but we have to build in disease and pest resistance," said IRRI director George Rothschild in a recent interview.
Scientists say the new thick-stalked variety can yield up to 12 or 13 tonnes per hectare (2-1/2 acres) and up to three crops per year.
BUDGET CUTS MAY HAMPER RESEARCH
The IRRI hopes to perfect the new strain by the turn of the century, but fears that cuts in its budget may hold up research.
"We may have a $6 million budget shortfall next year, which means we have to contract our resources severely. That could jeopardise our research," Rothschild said.
The IRRI needs $31 million to operate annually, a measly sum considering the benefits possible, he said.
"It (the budget cut) will affect our efficiency. We will have less people to work with. Our productivity will go down," said IRRI's principal plant breeder Gurdev Singh Khush.
Nevertheless, Rothschild said IRRI will see to it that the super-rice project gets priority despite budget cuts by traditional donors.
"I think the rest of the world is so preoccupied with domestic issues. They don't realise the importance of agriculture to economic development," he said.
"Many spend so much on the military. The cost of one fighter plane is more than many years of research in this institute. It's all a question of priorities."

Khush, head of the plant breeding, genetics and biochemistry division developing the new plant type, said his department is racing against time to introduce additional "characters" to the potential super-rice.
Besides building disease resistance into the new rice plant, genetics engineers at IRRI said they are also improving the grain's flavour to match local tastes.
"This type is supposed to be grown in tropical and subtropical Asia, where the farmers like long, slender grains, so we are trying to improve the quality," said Khush.
The new plant type is an improved version of the semi-dwarf and high-yielding variety introduced to farmers in 1966.
FINDING A 'MIRACLE RICE'
Khush and former IRRI scientist Henry Beachell were named winners of the $200,000 World Food Prize last October for developing rice varieties that allowed Asia to feed itself.
Beachell developed the "miracle rice" that doubled yields while Khush was responsible for the early-maturing, high-yielding variety that is now the most widely planted type.
Khush said IRRI did very well in the 1970s and the 1980s as rice production outpaced population increases in rice consuming countries.
"But in the 1990s, the trend has reversed. The population of rice consumers in Asia is growing by 1.8 percent every year while rice production is growing by 1.5 percent," he said.
Rice lands in Asia are also shrinking as farms are converted into residential, industrial or leisure areas.
As IRRI's scientists struggle to perfect the new variety, the prospect of budget cuts is the last thing they need to cope with, scientists said.
"If you (rice-eating countries) don't support research, how will we be able to (tackle) this challenge of feeding twice as many people in the space of just a generation?" Rothschild asked.
Development of a new rice plant variety takes up to 10 years, he said. "Even with new technology such as biotechnology, you can't do it cheap."
